lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Fall 2022. A university room full of students, laptops open, and a question on everyone's mind: what happens when your editor starts writing code alongside you?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That was right when AI pair programmers were brand new. Who hosted this?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Cédille, the consulting club at ÉTS, where students build real projects for outside clients. They invited GitHub and Arctiq to show Copilot and the AI tools around modern development, straight from people who ship the product.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So not rumors, but the actual tool.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. Students wanted to know where Copilot fits: internships, data labs, code review. Hearing it from the source cleared that up.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Three things. Copilot Chat, which explains and refactors code right in the editor, not just autocompletes. A command called createNotebook. And GitHub Next, a sandbox for experimental features.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It was the crowd favorite. You point Chat at a module in your repository, ask for a Jupyter notebook that imports and demonstrates it, and you get a first draft much faster than copying cells by hand. For courses and data exploration, that makes the blank notebook a lot less scary.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And the presenters did it on a real repo?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, no slideware only. They refactored a messy function in place: take the suggestion, check it, tweak it. Thierry Madkaud and Eldrick Wega presented, and the room was in a show-me-something-I-can-try-Monday mood.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What questions came from the audience?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Practical ones: what leaves your machine, who is responsible for the license of generated code, and whether it works offline. It doesn't, so Wi-Fi was part of the demo plan.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What did Antoine take home from it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Copilot is an accelerator, a fast first draft, while the person who commits stays the reviewer. Notebooks deserve to be taught together with Chat. And GitHub Next is a good place to preview features. His favorite first win for students is explaining unfamiliar code and generating test scaffolding.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A good habit to start with.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It is. The full write-up has photos of the room and links to his later diagram tooling.
